meeting_header: Date: 2025-05-09 14:00 PDT; Duration: 53 mins; Platform: Zoom; Redwood attendees: Maya Chen (AE), Ethan Park (Solutions Eng); Nimbus attendees: Jared Collins, Priya Desai, Tomoko Saito; Recording: enabled
summary: AE + SE ran a Console-focused demo showing request-level tracing, error and latency analysis, and debugging flows for a low-latency health-data inference workload. Team identified optimization opportunities (batching config and prefix/KV cache) and agreed to a short benchmark. Security questions about VPC/private control plane, SSO/SAML and audit logs were raised; AE to share compliance docs. SE will reproduce a slow tail request and surface policy-level fallback options.
topics: Debugging slow requests and tail latency
transcript: [00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. We'll do a short 50-ish minute deep dive into the Console's debugging flows, request insights, and how you'd troubleshoot tail latency. Ethan will drive the demo.

[00:00:18] Jared Collins: Thanks Maya, appreciate it. Quick context: we're processing clinical notes, fairly bursty traffic, and we have strict PII concerns. Our SLOs are tight around 200ms 95th percentile for short prompts.
[00:00:30] Ethan Park: Great, thanks Jared. We'll keep those numbers in mind. Priya, Tomoko, anything to add on infra constraints?
[00:00:41] Priya Desai: We run in a VPC and we want private control plane — not public-hosted. Also key mgmt via our KMS, SAML SSO for access. We'll want audit logs retained for 2 years ideally.
[00:01:02] Maya Chen: Perfect, we'll surface those controls in the security section; I have the SOC 2 and private deployment checklist ready to share after. Ethan, take it away.

[00:01:20] Ethan Park: Starting screen share — this is the Console. Top nav: Models, Routes, Traces, Requests, Optimize. We'll go to Traces first. Link: https://app.redwood.ai/console/trace/abc123 (demo link, ephemeral).

[00:02:05] Ethan Park: Traces show end-to-end request timelines — client->gateway->model. You can expand a trace to see per-step timing, token generation phases, and kernel execution. Note the orange spikes here — that's where the KV cache miss happened (transcript shows "KV cash" in quick note).
[00:02:32] Jared Collins: Can you show how to correlate that with the raw request log? We want to know which prompt caused the miss and if it was a bad prompt formatting or model mismatch.

[00:02:44] Ethan Park: Sure — jump to Requests tab and filter by request_id from the trace. You can see the payload, headers, model version, the route config used. Here we can also replay the request in a sandbox mode, or copy to a bench harness.
[00:03:12] Priya Desai: Is replay hitting the same hardware/quantization? We need fidelity for debugging noisy tails.

[00:03:25] Ethan Park: Good question — replay by default hits an isolated dev node that matches the production runtime profile. If you need exact CPU/GPU traces we can schedule a pinned run on Dedicated nodes as part of the pilot.
[00:04:03] Maya Chen: Quick qual check — are you expecting heavy embeddings in the same route or separate service? That changes batching config a lot.
[00:04:18] Jared Collins: Some routes do both — we glue embedding+completion in a single customer-facing endpoint which complicates batching.

[00:04:31] Ethan Park: That explains the tail — mixing short completions with long embedding calls creates head-of-line blocking. In Console Optimize we recommend isolating embeddings or using per-route batching policies; I can show the suggestion engine.

[00:05:02] Ethan Park: Switching to Optimize tab — here we ingest traffic profile and suggest batch sizes, max_latency targets, and quantization levels. For your profile we'd suggest smaller batch windows for completion routes and async embedding pipelines for vectorization-heavy flows.
[00:05:34] Tomoko Saito: How confident are those recommendations? Do you have numeric uplift examples?

[00:05:47] Ethan Park: Yes — we run simulations on your histogram input. Example: isolating embeddings reduced P95 by ~60% in a comparable customer case, and cost per 1k tokens dropped ~18% after switching to int8 quantization for the embedder model.
[00:06:20] Priya Desai: Show me how error analysis looks. We need to know if a model is hallucinating PHI or returning truncated results.

[00:06:34] Ethan Park: Jump back to a sample trace — open the error pane. You get the stack trace and the exact exception (e.g., "tokenization overflow" or OOM), plus the raw model output. There's a quick flag to redact PII in stored logs and to disable storing full responses — that ties into compliance.
[00:07:05] Jared Collins: We saw intermittent 500s yesterday. Can you surface where the issue was?

[00:07:18] Ethan Park: Looking at the traces from yesterday — most 500s correlate with an upstream model fallback policy that tried a larger model when the smaller one hit a generated token limit. Fallback resulted in queueing and occasional timeouts. Console shows the policy and you can change rollouts/disable fallback per route.

[00:07:50] Maya Chen: Important note: the fallback is intended for quality safety nets but can increase latency. For production you often prefer A/B deploys or canary with graceful degradation to a lower-cost variant rather than synchronous fallback.
[00:08:12] Tomoko Saito: Is there a simple way to see token-level cost per request?
[00:08:20] Ethan Park: Yes — expand the request and the cost tab shows token counts, model unit price, and a breakdown per stage. You can export CSVs for billing reconciliation.
[00:09:03] Priya Desai: Back to traces — can we annotate traces with our internal correlation IDs?
[00:09:12] Ethan Park: Absolutely — Console picks up X-Request-ID, X-Correlation-ID headers and surfaces them in traces/requests so you can cross-reference your internal logs.
[00:09:45] Jared Collins: Show a slow tail request walkthrough end-to-end.

[00:09:53] Ethan Park: Okay — here's a 95th percentile spike at 340ms. Expand it. Step 1: client -> network (15ms). Step 2: route pre-processing (25ms). Step 3: inference kernel time (280ms) with a sub-phase that's waiting on an external call — in this case a synchronous DB enrichment call from the customer side (transcription inferred: "DB enrichment" appears as an external call).
[00:10:32] Ethan Park: You can see the request log shows the payload and a callout to an external HTTP hook. In this demo that external call cost 220ms; if that were async we could shave the request.
[00:10:50] Priya Desai: That external call is in our code — good to know it surfaces. Can Console suggest code-level mitigations?

[00:11:02] Ethan Park: We provide runbooks in the Console that map common trace patterns to recommendations: move enrichment to async, add local cache, or use prefix cache on Redwood side. There's also an API to programmatically dump trace events for your observability stack.
[00:11:43] Jared Collins: Any gotchas with prefix caching? We've had cache staleness concerns with time-sensitive clinical data.

[00:11:52] Ethan Park: Prefix cache is TTL-based and you can scope it per-route. For sensitive data we recommend a conservative TTL or a per-tenant cache partitioning. Also, you can disable storage of prompt text and only cache embeddings.

[00:12:20] Maya Chen: Security quick aside — Priya you asked about audit logs retention. We support syslog/S3 exports and a built-in audit stream. We'll include the retention matrix in the SOC2 package.
[00:12:36] Priya Desai: Good, also need proof of SAML flows — can we get a test tenant for SSO validation?
[00:12:45] Maya Chen: Yes, we can provision a sandbox with SAML enabled for your engineers. We'll add that to next steps.

[00:13:05] Ethan Park: Back to demo: here's a live debug flow — mark a trace as "investigate" which opens a collaborative ticket. You can attach traces, add comments, and assign to an owner. Tickets sync to Jira via connector.
[00:13:37] Tomoko Saito: Do you keep the transcripts of model outputs in the ticket?
[00:13:43] Ethan Park: Optional — you can disable capturing outputs globally or per-route. For compliance, many customers opt to redact outputs and only store metadata and error traces.
[00:14:08] Jared Collins: Do you have RBAC that limits who can replay requests?
[00:14:16] Ethan Park: Yes — role-based controls for replay, trace viewing, and export. We integrate with SAML-based groups to map roles.
[00:15:02] Priya Desai: Walk me through how we'd run the benchmark you mentioned earlier.

[00:15:12] Ethan Park: We'll take your sample prompts, create a benchmark job in Console, pick a route and node profile (Dedicated or Hosted dev nodes), and run N requests at target concurrency. The output is latency histograms, error rates, and cost per 1k tokens. I'll run a 5k request sweep as an action item.

[00:16:05] Maya Chen: Quick pricing note — for pilots we can provide a time-limited Dedicated node pool at a discounted pilot rate; after pilot we'll recommend committed capacity if traffic justifies it.
[00:17:00] Jared Collins: Competitors wise — we evaluated the big public APIs but had concerns around data residency and predictability of latency. How do you compare on SLA and telemetry?

[00:17:15] Maya Chen: We publish performance profiles per model and region, and Dedicated comes with SLA-backed latency targets. The telemetry in Console gives you token-level cost and trace-level visibility which many managed APIs don't expose.
[00:18:10] Priya Desai: Any limitations on retention size for traces and request logs?
[00:18:17] Ethan Park: Hosted tier default 30 days; enterprise packages allow longer retention and S3 export. Private deployments can be configured to meet your retention needs on-prem.
[00:19:02] Tomoko Saito: About rollouts — can we do canary with automatic rollback on error spikes?
[00:19:10] Ethan Park: Yes — the rollout engine supports canary percentages and health checks. You can set rollback conditions based on error rate or latency thresholds.
[00:20:00] Jared Collins: For our stack, could Redwood integrate with our Datadog traces?
[00:20:08] Ethan Park: We have tracing hooks and can export trace events to Datadog or Honeycomb; also we ingest your correlation IDs to make cross-platform tracing easy.
[00:21:05] Priya Desai: If we go private deployment, how does upgrade/patching work?
[00:21:15] Maya Chen: Private deployments are customer-controlled with an optional Redwood-managed upgrade path. We ship signed artifacts and provide a rolling upgrade playbook.

[00:22:30] Ethan Park: Quick demo wrap: open an observed failure, drill to kernel stage, correlate with request logs and external calls, and create an investigation ticket. All done in under a minute in this example.
[00:23:10] Jared Collins: That was helpful — I like the replay and ticketing flow. My main remaining concern is pilot sizing and whether Dedicated is needed from day one.

[00:23:25] Ethan Park: For your traffic, recommended pilot: small Dedicated pool (2-4 GPUs) to validate tail performance, plus a plan to scale to 8-16 if the pilot shows linear growth. We'll size nodes after we see your benchmark.
[00:24:05] Maya Chen: Let's recap action items and next steps (we'll fast follow with docs). Any final quick q's?
[00:24:18] Tomoko Saito: Can you send an example of the CSV benchmark output and a sample billing reconciliation file?
[00:24:27] Maya Chen: Yes — Ethan will include sample reports. We'll also send the SOC2 and private deployment checklist.
[00:24:40] Priya Desai: One last: can we get a sandbox tenant with SAML to validate SSO flows before pilot?
[00:24:47] Maya Chen: Copy that — sandbox tenant with SAML, plus audit log samples, added to next steps.
[00:25:05] Jared Collins: Thanks all — we'll review and aim to provide traffic profiles and sample prompts by next Monday.
[00:25:14] Maya Chen: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the attachments and booking for the kickoff. End call.
[00:25:20] (recording stops)
